instructions: Translate each "en" text into the target language and put it in the "ka" field. Use "context" to choose the right meaning. Keep it natural and short; for vocab terms give the dictionary form. Leave the field empty if you are not sure. Do not change "key" or "en".

items.context: C2 n — A false belief, or an error in reasoning. Example: It is a fallacy that money guarantees happiness.
C2 n — A warning that something should be considered before acting or agreeing. Example: The forecast comes with an important caveat.
C2 v — To admit, often unwillingly, that something is true. Example: He conceded that he had made a mistake.
C2 n — A statement that says or proves that an argument or accusation is false. Example: The minister issued a firm rebuttal of the claims.
C2 n — An argument that opposes another argument. Example: A strong essay anticipates the main counterargument.
C2 v — To suggest that something is true as a basis for reasoning. Example: Einstein postulated that the speed of light is constant.
C2 n — An opinion or idea formed without complete information. Example: Much of what has been written about her is pure conjecture.
C2 adj — Based on guessing rather than on facts; also, risky for profit. Example: The report's conclusions are largely speculative.
C2 v — To use known facts to estimate what will happen or what is true in another situation. Example: You can't extrapolate national trends from one small town.
C2 n — Something that is different from what is normal or expected. Example: The results contained a statistical anomaly.
C2 n — A statement accepted as true without proof. Example: It is an axiom of economics that people respond to incentives.
C2 n — A sharp division between two opposing things. Example: The dichotomy between theory and practice is often exaggerated.
C2 n — A situation or statement with two parts that seem to contradict each other. Example: It's a paradox that the richest countries can feel the poorest.
C2 n — A conclusion reached on the basis of evidence and reasoning. Example: The obvious inference is that the system failed.
C2 n — The process of reaching a conclusion by reasoning from general facts. Example: By a simple deduction, she identified the error.
C2 v — To notice or understand something that is not obvious. Example: It was difficult to discern any pattern in the data.
C2 adj — Showing awareness of small but important differences. Example: The book offers a nuanced view of the conflict.
C2 adj — Having many small parts arranged in a complicated way. Example: The plot is intricate but rewarding.
C2 adj — Related to ideas and principles rather than practical details. Example: The project is still at the conceptual stage.
C2 v — To repeat an experiment or study and get the same results. Example: Other labs have been unable to replicate the findings.
C2 n — Careful and detailed examination. Example: The proposal will come under close scrutiny.
C2 n — A judgement of the value, quality or performance of someone or something. Example: Staff receive an annual performance appraisal.
C2 adj — Seeming to be everywhere at the same time. Example: Smartphones have become ubiquitous.
C2 n — A written law passed by a parliament. Example: The right is protected by statute.
C2 n — A person who brings a case against someone in a court of law. Example: The court ruled in favour of the plaintiff.
C2 n — An official decision in a court case; also, an opinion after judging something. Example: The jury returned a verdict of not guilty.
C2 n — A special court or group of people with authority to judge a particular type of dispute. Example: She took her case to an employment tribunal.
C2 n — The settling of a dispute by an independent person or group. Example: The dispute went to arbitration.
C2 n — A separate section of a legal document; also, a group of words with a subject and verb. Example: The contract contains a confidentiality clause.
C2 n — A condition in a legal agreement or law; also, the act of supplying something. Example: The law includes provisions for appeals.
C2 n — The act of obeying a rule, law or request. Example: All products must be in compliance with safety standards.
C2 n — The process of making sure that laws or rules are obeyed. Example: Stricter enforcement of speed limits is needed.
C2 n — Failure to take proper care, especially when this is a legal duty. Example: The hospital was sued for negligence.
C2 n — An act of breaking a law, promise or agreement. Example: Failing to deliver on time is a breach of contract.
C2 n — Protection against financial loss, or payment for loss or damage. Example: The policy provides indemnity against legal costs.
C2 n — The power of a country to govern itself. Example: The treaty respects national sovereignty.
C2 n — The authority given to a government or organisation to act. Example: The government has a clear mandate for reform.
C2 v — To make an agreement official by signing or voting for it. Example: The treaty was ratified by all member states.
C2 n — The official right to refuse to allow something. Example: The president used his veto to block the bill.
C2 n — A system of government or management with many complicated rules. Example: Small firms complain about excessive bureaucracy.
C2 n — A right or privilege that belongs to a particular person or group. Example: Choosing the team is the manager's prerogative.
C2 adj — Allowed by law; also, reasonable and justifiable. Example: They raised legitimate concerns about safety.
C2 n — A system in which people or things are ranked according to importance. Example: She rose quickly through the company hierarchy.
C2 n — A policy of strict cuts in government spending. Example: Years of austerity have left public services stretched.
C2 n — The availability of cash, or how easily an asset can be turned into cash. Example: The bank faced a liquidity crisis.
C2 n — The state of having enough money to pay all debts. Example: Investors began to doubt the company's solvency.
C2 n — Property promised to a lender as a guarantee that a loan will be repaid. Example: He used his house as collateral for the loan.
C2 n — The use of borrowed money to increase possible returns; also, power to influence. Example: The deal gave the union more leverage in negotiations.
C2 n — The value of shares in a company; also, fairness. Example: The founders hold 60% of the equity.
C2 n — A collection of investments; also, a set of examples of someone's work. Example: She has a diversified investment portfolio.
C2 n — The tendency to change suddenly and unpredictably. Example: Market volatility has increased this year.
C2 n — A situation in which there is no growth or development. Example: The economy suffered a decade of stagnation.
C2 n — A fall in the value of something over time. Example: The depreciation of the currency made imports more expensive.
C2 n — A raw material or product that can be bought and sold, such as oil or wheat. Example: Commodity prices fell sharply.
C2 n — A share of a company's profits paid to shareholders. Example: The company announced a higher dividend.
C2 n — The amount by which spending is greater than income. Example: The budget deficit has doubled.
C2 adj — Relating to money, especially the money supply in a country. Example: The central bank tightened monetary policy.
C2 v — To change frequently in level or amount. Example: Prices fluctuate according to demand.
C2 v — To pay out money from a fund. Example: The grant will be disbursed in three instalments.
C2 v — To combine into a single, stronger unit; also, to make a position stronger. Example: The firm consolidated its debts into one loan.
C2 v — To develop a wider range of products, investments or activities. Example: Farmers are diversifying into tourism.
C2 adj — Relating to beauty and artistic taste. Example: The design has great aesthetic appeal.
C2 n — A story or a description of events; also, a way of explaining events. Example: The film follows a non-linear narrative.
C2 n — A type of art, music, film or writing with a particular style. Example: Crime fiction is her favourite genre.
C2 n — A word or phrase used to describe something by comparing it to something else. Example: 'A sea of troubles' is a metaphor.
C2 n — A feeling or idea suggested by a word in addition to its basic meaning. Example: 'Cheap' has negative connotations; 'inexpensive' does not.
C2 n — A detailed analysis and judgement of something. Example: The essay offers a sharp critique of consumer culture.
C2 adj — Famous and respected. Example: The museum is renowned for its collection of icons.
C2 adj — Respected and admired as very important or of high quality. Example: She won a prestigious literary prize.
C2 adj — Famous for something bad. Example: The road is notorious for accidents.
C2 adj — Very old and no longer used; old-fashioned. Example: The poem uses archaic language.
C2 adj — Lasting for a long time or happening again and again. Example: Traffic is a perennial problem in the city.
C2 adj — Bringing strong images, memories or feelings to mind. Example: The novel opens with an evocative description of the sea.
C2 adj — Clever and quick to see how to gain an advantage. Example: She is an astute businesswoman.
C2 adj — Very careful and paying great attention to detail. Example: He keeps meticulous records.
C2 adj — Very careful to be honest and do what is right; also, very thorough. Example: She was scrupulous about declaring every expense.
C2 adj — Careful to do your work well and thoroughly. Example: He is a conscientious and reliable employee.
C2 adj — Sensible and careful when making decisions, avoiding unnecessary risks. Example: It would be prudent to save some money.
C2 adj — Too satisfied with yourself, so that you do not try harder or see dangers. Example: We cannot afford to be complacent about safety.
C2 adj — Lacking experience and too ready to believe others. Example: It would be naive to expect quick results.
C2 adj — Openly refusing to obey or show respect. Example: He remained defiant despite the criticism.
C2 adj — Able to recover quickly from difficulties. Example: Children are often remarkably resilient.
C2 n — The quality of continuing to try hard and not giving up. Example: Her tenacity eventually paid off.
C2 n — The ability to make good judgements and quick decisions, especially in business. Example: He is known for his business acumen.
C2 n — The quality of not thinking you are better than other people. Example: Despite her success, she spoke with great humility.
C2 adj — Generous and kind, especially towards a rival or someone who has treated you badly. Example: She was magnanimous in victory.
C2 n — The ability to understand and share another person's feelings. Example: Good doctors show empathy towards their patients.
C2 n — A feeling of anger because you have been treated unfairly. Example: There is growing resentment over the new tax.
C2 n — Anger caused by something that seems unfair. Example: The decision provoked widespread indignation.
C2 n — A feeling of pleasure mixed with sadness when thinking about the past. Example: The song filled her with nostalgia.
C2 n — A feeling of great happiness and excitement. Example: The euphoria of victory did not last long.
C2 n — A feeling of fear or anxiety about something that may happen. Example: She opened the letter with some trepidation.
C2 n — A feeling of being satisfied with your situation so that you do not try to improve it. Example: Complacency is the enemy of progress.
C2 v — To increase rapidly in number or amount. Example: Online courses have proliferated in recent years.
C2 v — To go beyond the usual limits of something. Example: Great music transcends cultural boundaries.
C2 v — To learn and understand information completely; also, to become part of a group. Example: It takes time to assimilate so much new information.
C2 v — To spread information or knowledge so that it reaches many people. Example: The results were disseminated through academic journals.
C2 v — To increase the size, amount or value of something by adding to it. Example: She augments her salary by teaching in the evenings.
C2 v — To make something stronger or louder; also, to add details. Example: Social media can amplify misinformation.
C2 v — To make something bad happen suddenly or sooner. Example: The scandal precipitated the minister's resignation.
C2 v — To support or form the basis of an argument, system or theory. Example: Strong values underpin the company's success.
C2 v — To support or strengthen something. Example: The good news bolstered investors' confidence.
C2 v — To slow down or stop the progress of something. Example: Bad weather impeded the rescue efforts.
C2 v — To prevent something from happening or someone from doing something. Example: His injury precludes him from playing.
C2 v — To replace something older or less effective. Example: The old model has been superseded by a faster one.
C2 v — To find a way of avoiding a rule or difficulty. Example: They circumvented the regulations by registering abroad.
C2 v — To involve something as a necessary part or result. Example: The job entails a lot of travel.
C2 v — To make a bad situation better. Example: Measures were taken to ameliorate working conditions.
C2 v — To place things side by side, especially to compare or contrast them. Example: The exhibition juxtaposes ancient and modern art.
C2 n — A big change that causes a lot of disruption. Example: The country went through a period of political upheaval.
C2 n — A state of great confusion or uncertainty. Example: The markets were in turmoil after the announcement.
C2 n — The path or course of development of something. Example: Her career has followed an upward trajectory.
C2 n — The level at which something starts to happen or have an effect. Example: Earnings above this threshold are taxed at 40%.
C2 n — A situation in which no progress is possible. Example: Negotiations have reached an impasse.
C2 n — A possible result of an action, often complicated or unexpected. Example: Have you considered the legal ramifications?
C2 n — Someone or something that causes an important change. Example: The crisis acted as a catalyst for reform.
C2 n — A possible future event that must be prepared for. Example: We have a contingency plan in case of delays.
C2 adj — So small or unimportant that it is not worth considering. Example: The difference in cost is negligible.
C2 adj — Very noticeable. Example: There has been a marked improvement in her work.
C2 adj — Not safe or certain; likely to change for the worse. Example: Many freelancers live in a precarious financial situation.
C2 adj — Likely to change suddenly and unexpectedly, often for the worse. Example: The situation in the region remains volatile.
C2 adj — No longer used because something newer exists. Example: Fax machines are almost obsolete.
C2 adj — Lasting for a long time. Example: The book has enduring appeal.
C2 adj — Existing or most common at a particular time. Example: The prevailing view is that rates will rise.
C2 adj — Based on ideas rather than practical experience. Example: The risk is purely theoretical.
C2 adj — Imagined or suggested but not necessarily real or true. Example: Let's consider a hypothetical example.
C2 adj — Including everyone or everything; not leaving anyone out. Example: The school aims to be inclusive of all abilities.
C2 adv — Apparently or according to what is claimed, but perhaps not really. Example: He was there, ostensibly, to help.
C2 adv — In a way that cannot be avoided. Example: Inevitably, the changes caused some confusion.
C2 adv — In a clear and absolute way. Example: The company categorically denies the allegations.
C2 adv — In a way that leaves no doubt. Example: The evidence points unequivocally to fraud.
C2 adv — Until now or until a particular time. Example: The method solves a hitherto unsolved problem.
C2 adv — From this time on. Example: Henceforth, all applications must be submitted online.
C2 adv — Of the thing just mentioned. Example: The contract, or any part thereof, may not be copied.
C2 phr — Despite what has just been stated. Example: Notwithstanding the above, exceptions may be made in urgent cases.
C2 phr — For the same reason; in a similar way. Example: Prices may rise; by the same token, they may also fall.
C2 phr — Understanding a situation only after it has happened. Example: With the benefit of hindsight, we should have acted sooner.
C2 phr — In every important way; virtually. Example: To all intents and purposes, the war was over.
C2 phr — A matter that is uncertain or no longer relevant to discuss. Example: Whether he would have agreed is now a moot point.
C2 phr — The most important or central part of a problem. Example: The crux of the matter is who will pay.
C2 phr — To cause doubt about something. Example: The new evidence calls his account into question.
C2 phr — To say you support something without doing anything to help it. Example: Many companies only pay lip service to diversity.
C2 phr — To do something that will be used as an example for future decisions. Example: The ruling could set a precedent for similar cases.

items.en: to err on the side of caution
items.context: C2 phr — To be extra careful rather than take a risk. Example: We erred on the side of caution and cancelled the trip.
C2 phr — To argue about very small, unimportant differences. Example: Let's not split hairs over the exact wording.

items.en: to have a vested interest in
items.context: C2 phr — To have a personal reason, often financial, for wanting something to happen. Example: The authors have a vested interest in the drug's success.
C2 phr — A result that is certain before it happens. Example: The outcome of the vote was a foregone conclusion.
C2 phr — To behave very formally. Example: Please don't stand on ceremony; call me Anna.

items.en: Yes, I am. My name is Nino. Nice to meet you.
items.context: A1 dialogue "Meeting a new classmate", you speaking
